# The Lantern Archive

The Lantern Archive stands at the edge of the old harbor, where the stone quay
turns north and the warehouses give way to narrow houses. It was built as a
customs hall, but its tall windows and dry upper rooms made it more useful as a
store for charts, court records, and ships' journals. [[Mara Venn]], the current
keeper, opens the public room shortly after sunrise and closes it when the lamps
are lit along the quay. Visitors describe the place as quiet rather than grand.

Most people arrive with a practical question. They want the former name of a
street, the owner of a lost vessel, or the date when a boundary stone was moved.
Mara begins with the harbor ledgers and works outward from there. Each answer
usually uncovers another small uncertainty: a copied surname, a missing page, or
a witness whose account does not agree with the official record. The archive is
valuable because it keeps those disagreements visible instead of smoothing them
away.

Short notes are kept beside the main catalog.

They record corrections that have not yet earned a permanent entry.

## The Reading Room

The reading room occupies the center of the building. Six oak tables stand
beneath a ceiling crossed by plain iron braces, and every chair faces enough
daylight to read faded ink without a lamp. The walls carry no portraits. Shelves
rise only to shoulder height, leaving the room open and easy to survey. A clerk
can therefore help a visitor without hovering, while a visitor can work for an
hour without feeling watched.

Requests are written on blue cards and placed in a shallow tray. A clerk checks
the shelf mark, retrieves the item, and records its condition before bringing it
to the table. This routine is slower than allowing readers into the stacks, but
it has prevented the gradual disorder that ruined the earlier collection at
[[North Gate House]]. The cards also create a useful history of which records
people consult and which subjects have fallen out of memory.

The room's rules are brief:

- Pencils may be used, but ink stays at the clerk's desk.
- Bound volumes rest on supports and are never forced flat.
- Loose papers remain in their numbered order.
- Food, drink, and wet coats stay in the entrance hall.

> A record is useful only when the next reader can find it in the same state.

### A Normal Morning

On an ordinary morning, the first visitor is often a harbor official checking a
registration detail before the day's hearings. Students arrive later and choose
tables near the windows. Messengers come and go with sealed requests from offices
that cannot spare a clerk. Around noon, the room briefly empties. Mara uses that
quiet interval to return volumes, sharpen pencils, and add yesterday's cards to
the request index.

The work is repetitive, but not mechanical. A familiar place name may conceal
three different sites, and a ship may have changed owners without changing its
name. Clerks are trained to state what a record proves, what it merely suggests,
and what remains unknown. That distinction matters most when a visitor arrives
already convinced of the answer. The archive does not settle every argument; it
shows which parts of an argument have evidence.

## Finding a Record

The public catalog is organized by subject, place, and date. Names appear in a
separate index because spelling changed often during the archive's first century.
Someone searching for [[Elias Tor]] may also need to check Elias Torr, E. Tor,
and the household entry for the eastern ropewalk. Cross-references are written in
full rather than represented by unexplained symbols. This consumes more paper,
but it saves time for readers who use the catalog only occasionally.

A basic search follows three steps:

1. Start with the broad subject card and note the collection identifiers.
2. Check the place or name index for alternate terms and older spellings.
3. Ask a clerk to compare the resulting shelf marks with the closed-stack list.

Some references point to records that are no longer present. The catalog retains
these entries, including the unresolved reference to [[The Glass Pilot]], because
removing them would hide the shape of the former collection. A missing record can
still establish that a survey was made, a hearing took place, or a report once
circulated. Its absence is evidence of a different kind, provided the catalog is
clear about what survives.

### Copies and Corrections

Readers may order handwritten or photographic copies. Every copy includes the
collection name, shelf mark, page number, and date of production. Obvious damage
is not repaired in the copy, and unclear words are not silently completed. When a
clerk supplies a likely reading, it appears in brackets with the clerk's initials.
This practice can make a transcript look busy, but it allows later researchers to
separate the old text from a modern judgment.

Corrections follow the same principle. The original catalog card remains in
place, while a new card explains the error and points back to the source used to
correct it. Particularly important changes are reviewed by two clerks. Minor
spelling corrections require only one reviewer, though the date and initials are
still recorded. Nothing depends on remembering who changed a label years after
the fact.

## The Upper Stacks

The upper floor is closed to visitors. Its shelves hold salt-stained logbooks,
rolled plans, boxes of correspondence, and the administrative records of the
archive itself. Light enters through shutters that can be narrowed during bright
weather. Small brass labels mark each bay, and a painted line on the floor keeps
carts from striking the lowest shelves. The arrangement is plain because every
decoration competes with the signs clerks actually need.

Twice each year, the staff checks one complete row from end to end. They compare
the shelf contents with the catalog, note damaged enclosures, and move nothing
until discrepancies have been recorded. The inspection rarely produces a
dramatic discovery. Its value lies in catching ordinary drift before it becomes
loss: one folder returned to the neighboring box, one label loosened by damp, or
one plan rolled around the wrong core.

## Closing Notes

At the end of the day, open volumes return to the stacks and unfinished requests
move to a separate tray. The clerks cover the reading tables, close the shutters,
and leave one lamp burning at the entrance until the last visitor has collected a
coat or parcel. Mara then writes a short entry in the daily book. Most entries are
only a few lines, yet together they show how the archive is used in a way the
formal catalog never could.

The building succeeds through accumulated restraint. Its rooms do not demand
attention, its procedures do not pretend to eliminate judgment, and its records
are allowed to contain uncertainty. People come because they can read, compare,
and revise their understanding without being hurried. The archive offers no
spectacle. It offers a dependable place to think.
